elements: plain white horizontal background field
five identical black wireframe camera-frustum icons arranged in a straight horizontal row
for each of the five camera icons: one solid black circular projection center dot near the bottom of the icon

interactions.label: Build the lateral-translation strip

demo_steps.title: Identical camera orientations
demo_steps.narration: The five black wireframe cameras are copies of the same icon, evenly spaced in a row. Their frusta all point the same way, so the camera is not rotating between positions.

demo_steps.title: Sideways motion cue
demo_steps.narration: A single red horizontal arrow is added between two camera positions. It points across the strip, perpendicular to the drawn viewing frustum direction.

demo_steps.title: Lateral translation sequence
demo_steps.narration: All six red arrows are shown, each with the same size and rightward direction. The full strip represents repeated sideways camera positions with zero forward velocity component.

plan.geometry_notes: Use a flat front-on orthographic composition on the XY plane with no perspective depth. Overall visible field about 12.5 world units wide by 2.6 world units high, white background #ffffff. Coordinate convention: +X is screen-right, +Y is screen-up, Z is only for render layering and should not create visible 3D perspective. Place the five camera icons at x = -4.4, -2.2, 0, 2.2, 4.4 with identical y placement and identical scale. Each camera icon occupies about 1.05 units wide by 1.45 units tall. For each icon, projection center dot is a filled black circle radius 0.105 at local (0, -0.62). Image plane rectangle is centered at local (0, 0.32), width 0.95, height 0.52, with its long edges perfectly horizontal and vertical sides upright. Rectangle corners: (-0.475, 0.06), (0.475, 0.06), (0.475, 0.58), (-0.475, 0.58). Draw four straight black line segments from the dot center to all four rectangle corners. Draw the rectangle outline itself in black. Draw internal black crossing lines within or across the image-plane rectangle: from upper-left corner to lower-right corner and from upper-right corner to lower-left corner, matching the bold symbolic crossed-plane look. All camera line strokes black #000000, visually heavy, about 4 px, with round line caps and joins where possible. Red arrows are pure red #ff0000, identical, horizontal, and located at y = -0.63, aligned with the camera-dot baseline. Use six arrows with start/end x ranges approximately: [-6.1, -5.2], [-3.55, -2.65], [-1.35, -0.45], [0.85, 1.75], [3.05, 3.95], [5.25, 6.15]. Each arrow has a thick rectangular shaft about 0.09 world units high and a filled triangular arrowhead about 0.26 units long by 0.28 units high, pointing exactly right. In buildPhase=camerasOnly show only the five black camera icons. In buildPhase=singleDirectionCue show the five camera icons plus only the central red arrow between the middle pair of cameras. In buildPhase=completeStrip show all five camera icons and all six red arrows. Do not include near/far points, projection rays to scene points, optical-flow vectors, halos, ghost overlays, axes, path curves, inset plots, or explanatory text labels in the default completeStrip view.
plan.notes: Render as a 2D vector-like diagram using an orthographic camera looking straight at the XY plane; lock orbit/rotation and use no perspective convergence. Use TubeGeometry, fat-line rendering, or screen-space line widths so the black outlines and red arrows stay bold at PDF-reader scale. Keep all camera copies exactly equal in size and orientation; do not shrink objects with x-position. Layer red arrows slightly behind or below camera outlines only if overlap occurs, but preserve the clean horizontal strip.

authoredPrompt: This figure is a horizontal strip in which the same wireframe camera appears five times, evenly spaced across a white field and interleaved with thick red arrows. Each camera is a viewing frustum seen from behind and slightly below: a solid black dot at the bottom marks the projection center, four straight edges rise from it to the corners of a wide rectangle standing for the image plane, and lines cross that rectangle to its lower corners, so the pyramid reads as pointing up and away from the viewer. The five copies match exactly in size and orientation. Red arrows run horizontally along the base of the strip, one before the leftmost camera, one in each of the four gaps, and one trailing off the right edge, every arrowhead pointing right. Because the frusta aim away from the viewer while the arrows travel across the picture, the motion is perpendicular to the line of sight rather than along it. The sequence illustrates sideways camera motion parallel to the image plane, as when a scene slides past the side window of a moving car, in which the forward velocity component is zero.
authoredInteractions:
- Animation for sliding the camera sideways parallel to the image plane; the frustum translates across the strip while projected scene points shift laterally, showing motion with zero forward component.
- Slider for lateral displacement; the active camera moves from left to right and image-plane vectors lengthen with the displacement, making the relation between side motion and apparent image shift explicit.
- Toggle between the 3-D path and projected optical flow for near versus far points; the flow view shows larger shifts for nearer points, connecting lateral translation to depth-dependent parallax.
authoredContext:
Consider a camera translating laterally, as shown in
the figure. This will happen if you are looking
through a side window of a car at the scene passing by. In this case,
the forward velocity is zero, $V_Z=0$.

Lateral camera motion parallel to the camera plane.

interactions.label: Animate lateral translation
interactions.teaches: The camera translates sideways across the strip while its viewing direction stays fixed, so the motion has no forward component along the optical axis

interactions.label: Lateral displacement
interactions.teaches: Increasing sideways displacement produces increasing image displacement on the projection plane, making apparent motion proportional to camera side motion

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Comparing the physical camera path with image-plane flow shows that lateral translation creates depth-dependent parallax: nearer points shift more than farther points

demo_steps.title: Sideways camera path
demo_steps.narration: The camera copies form a left-to-right strip, and every red arrow points horizontally. The frustum orientation does not change, so the camera is translating parallel to the image plane rather than moving forward.

demo_steps.title: Displace the active camera
demo_steps.narration: Move the active frustum to the right. The camera center shifts laterally while the rectangular image plane remains parallel to its starting pose.

demo_steps.title: Optical flow from lateral motion
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the projection view. The near point’s image vector is visibly longer than the far point’s vector, showing the inverse-depth dependence of lateral-motion parallax.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a wide horizontal composition like the source: overall strip about 12 world units wide by 2.2 units high on a white background. Coordinate convention: +X is screen-right and is the lateral camera-translation direction; +Y is screen-up; +Z is the camera optical axis receding away from the viewer. Recreate five camera frusta at X = -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, all identical in size and orientation. Each frustum has projection center as a black sphere/circle radius about 0.11 at local (0, -0.55, 0). The image plane is a black wire rectangle centered at local (0, 0.45, 0.75), width 0.95, height 0.55, with its long edge horizontal and its vertical sides upright. Draw black line segments from the projection center to all four image-plane corners; the two lines to the top corners form the strong inverted V seen in the source, and the two lines to the lower corners form the shorter lower V. Stroke color black #000000, stroke width visually heavy, about 4 px. Red arrows are saturated #ff0000, thick shafts about 0.08 world units high with triangular arrowheads; place them horizontally at Y about -0.65, one before the first camera, one in each gap, and one exiting the right edge. Each arrow length about 1.2 world units, shaft horizontal, arrowhead to the right. For the active interactive frustum, use the same geometry and place it at X = lateralDisplacement, with ghost frusta in light gray/black opacity 0.25 at the five sampled positions. Near and far scene points for the flow comparison can be fixed in front of the starting camera at world coordinates approximately Pnear = (0.6, 0.1, 2.0) and Pfar = (0.6, 0.1, 5.0). Use pinhole projection u = f * (Xpoint - Xcamera) / Zpoint with f = 1.0 on a flat image plane; for equal lateral camera displacement T, image shift magnitude is |Δu| = f * |T| / Z, so the near-point vector must be about 2.5 times the far-point vector for Znear = 2 and Zfar = 5. Near point color orange #ff9900; far point color blue #3366cc; near flow vector red/orange and longer; far flow vector blue and shorter.
interactionPlan.notes: Keep the main default view visually close to the source strip: repeated black frusta with red rightward arrows, no perspective convergence, and generous horizontal whitespace. Implement the animation by driving lateralDisplacement sinusoidally or linearly from -4 to 4 and looping. In Projected optical flow mode, flatten to an image-plane inset or replace the 3-D frustum emphasis with a rectangular image plane showing before/after projected point positions and arrows; keep the source-like strip faintly visible so the learner connects the flow view to the same lateral camera motion.

attempts.html:
Demo steps
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: The source is a flat horizontal strip of five identical camera icons with red arrows between them, while the generated view shows the strip receding diagonally in a 3D axonometric view.
The generated figure adds near/far points, projection rays, projected image points, an optical-flow inset, ghost cameras, and explanatory labels that are not present in the source.
The red arrows in the source are large, uniform, horizontal arrows spanning the gaps; in the generated figure they are smaller, tilted by the camera view, and partly mixed with 3D path elements.
The camera icons are much smaller and more cluttered than the bold simple black outlines in the source, reducing the clean repeated-symbol appearance.
The source has no text labels, while the generated output overlays multiple labels such as 'sideways camera translation' and optical-flow explanations.
The generated composition includes an active highlighted camera and translucent path/ghost elements, which changes the simple static sequence shown in the source.
evaluation.notes: The repeated camera-and-arrow motif is present, but the generated figure overinterprets the simple flat source as a 3D optical-flow teaching scene with many extra elements and labels.
action_items: Use a front-on orthographic view so the five camera icons and red arrows form a straight horizontal strip like the source.
Remove the near/far points, projection rays, optical-flow inset, active halo, ghost overlays, and explanatory labels from the default view.
Enlarge and simplify the black camera outlines and red arrows to match the bold, clean proportions of the source figure.
Keep all red arrows horizontal, uniform in size, and positioned between the camera icons at the same vertical level as in the reference.
plan_action_items: Revise the plan to reproduce the flat symbolic lateral-translation strip rather than expanding it into a full 3D parallax/optical-flow demonstration.

feedback.rationale: The critic identifies hallucinated 3D parallax/optical-flow content and explicitly calls for revising the plan to reproduce the flat symbolic camera-arrow strip, indicating a conceptual planning error rather than just implementation polish.

discrepancies: The camera-and-arrow strip is much smaller and placed low in the canvas, whereas the source fills the height more and sits near the top edge.
The red arrows are shorter with larger gaps between arrows and cameras; in the source the arrows span farther across the strip and extend to the image edges.
The red arrow centerline is slightly below the camera lens centers, while the source arrows align more closely with the lens/camera-center level.
The generated view includes a large explanatory control panel that is absent from the source and visually changes the simple wide-strip composition.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure correctly recreates the five flat camera icons and six rightward red arrows, but the scale, vertical placement, and arrow spacing are noticeably less faithful to the source.
action_items: Scale the camera strip up vertically and position it closer to the top edge to match the source banner composition.
Lengthen the red arrows so they span more of each gap and extend closer to the left and right edges.
Align the red arrow shafts precisely with the black lens/camera-center points.
Reduce the visual dominance of the control panel or keep the default figure area closer to the source's wide uninterrupted strip.
